explanation.title: Spanish Pronouns: Subject, Object, Reflexive & More

sections.subtitle: Subject Pronouns & Pro-drop
sections.content:
👥 Subject Pronouns

Singular:
• yo → I
• tú → you (informal)
• él/ella → he/she
• usted → you (formal)

Plural:
• nosotros/nosotras → we
• vosotros/vosotras → you (plural, Spain)
• ellos/ellas → they
• ustedes → you (plural formal/Latin America)

💡 'Pro-drop' Language

Verb endings show subject → often omit pronoun:
• Hablo español (I speak Spanish)
  ❌ NOT Yo hablo español

✅ Use pronouns for:
• Emphasis → YO hablo español
• Clarification → Él habla, ella no

sections.subtitle: Direct Object Pronouns
sections.content:
🎯 Direct Object (receives action directly)

Pronouns:
• me → me
• te → you
• lo → him/it/you formal (masc)
• la → her/it/you formal (fem)
• nos → us
• os → you plural (Spain)
• los → them/you plural (masc)
• las → them/you plural (fem)

Example:
• Veo el libro → Lo veo
  (I see the book → I see it)

📍 Placement:
• BEFORE conjugated verbs
  → Lo veo
• Attached to infinitives/gerunds/commands
  → Quiero verlo (I want to see it)
  → Viéndolo (seeing it)

sections.subtitle: Indirect Object Pronouns
sections.content:
🎯 Indirect Object (TO WHOM/FOR WHOM)

Pronouns:
• me → to me
• te → to you
• le → to him/her/you formal
• nos → to us
• os → to you plural (Spain)
• les → to them/you plural

Examples:
• Le doy el libro
  → I give the book to him/her
• Me compra flores
  → He buys flowers for me

💡 Redundant use (common!):
• Le doy el libro a María
  → I give the book to María
  (le is redundant but used for clarity)

sections.subtitle: Combined Object Pronouns
sections.content:
🔗 Using BOTH Pronouns Together

Order: INDIRECT + DIRECT

⚠️ Special rule:
le/les + lo/la/los/las → se + lo/la/los/las

Examples:
• Le doy el libro (I give him the book)
  → Se lo doy (I give it to him)

• Les mando las cartas (I send them the letters)
  → Se las mando (I send them to them)

📍 Placement rules:
• Both BEFORE conjugated verb
  → Se lo digo
• Both attached to infinitive/gerund/command
  → Quiero dárselo
  → Diciéndoselo

✅ Both pronouns stay together!

sections.subtitle: Reflexive Pronouns
sections.content:
🤷 Subject Acts on Itself

Pronouns:
• me → myself
• te → yourself
• se → himself/herself/yourself formal/themselves
• nos → ourselves
• os → yourselves (Spain)

Used with reflexive verbs:

• Me lavo → I wash myself
• Te levantas → You get (yourself) up
• Se llama Pedro → He calls himself Pedro
  (His name is Pedro)
• Nos vestimos → We dress ourselves

✅ Pronoun MUST match subject:
• yo  → me
• tú → te
• él/ella/usted → se
• nosotros → nos

sections.subtitle: Other Important Pronouns
sections.content:
💼 Possessive Pronouns

• el mío/la mía → mine
• el tuyo/la tuya → yours
• el suyo/la suya → his/hers/yours/theirs
• el nuestro/la nuestra → ours

👉 Demonstrative

• éste/ésta → this one
• ése/ésa → that one
• aquél/aquélla → that one (far)

❓ Interrogative

• ¿qué? → what?
• ¿quién/quiénes? → who?
• ¿cuál/cuáles? → which?

🧑 Indefinite

• alguien → someone
• nadie → no one
• algo → something
• nada → nothing

questions.question: What is the subject pronoun for 'I' in Spanish?
questions.hint: This is the first person singular subject pronoun, though it's often omitted in Spanish.

questions.question: What is the informal 'you' (singular) in Spanish?
questions.hint: This has an accent mark. Don't confuse with 'tu' (your) without accent.

questions.question: What is the formal 'you' (singular) in Spanish?
questions.hint: This is used for formal/respectful situations. Often abbreviated as 'Ud.'

questions.question: Why can you say 'Hablo español' without 'yo'?

answers.text: Spanish is pro-drop - verb endings show the subject
Subject pronouns don't exist in Spanish
You must always omit subject pronouns

questions.hint: The verb ending '-o' already indicates 'I', so the subject pronoun is optional unless emphasizing.

questions.question: What direct object pronoun replaces 'el libro' (the book)?
questions.hint: Libro is masculine singular. Use the masculine singular direct object pronoun.

questions.question: How do you say 'I see it' (referring to 'el libro')?
questions.hint: The direct object pronoun goes BEFORE the conjugated verb.

questions.question: What direct object pronoun replaces 'las casas' (the houses)?
questions.hint: Casas is feminine plural. Use the feminine plural direct object pronoun.

questions.question: What does 'Le doy el libro' mean?

answers.text: I give the book to him/her/you (formal)
I give him the book (direct object)

questions.hint: 'Le' is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/her/you formal'.

questions.question: What is the indirect object pronoun for 'to me'?
questions.hint: This is the same form as the direct object pronoun 'me', but functions as indirect.

questions.question: What happens to 'le' when combined with 'lo'?
questions.hint: When 'le/les' comes before 'lo/la/los/las', it changes to 'se' to avoid saying two similar sounds.

questions.question: How do you say 'I give it to him' (libro = book)?
questions.hint: Le → se before lo. Order: se lo + verb. 'Se' = to him, 'lo' = it (the book).

questions.question: What does 'Me lavo' mean?
questions.hint: 'Me' is a reflexive pronoun here - the subject (I) acts on itself.

questions.question: What is the reflexive pronoun for 'himself/herself/themselves'?
questions.hint: This is used for third person reflexive (él se lava, ellos se lavan).

questions.question: What does 'Se llama Pedro' mean?

answers.text: His name is Pedro / He calls himself Pedro

questions.hint: 'Llamarse' is a reflexive verb meaning 'to be called/named'.

questions.question: How do you say 'mine' (referring to a masculine object)?
questions.hint: Possessive pronouns need an article. Use 'el' for masculine singular objects.

questions.question: What does '¿Quién es?' mean?
questions.hint: '¿Quién?' is the interrogative pronoun for 'who?'

questions.question: What does '¿Qué es?' mean?
questions.hint: '¿Qué?' asks about the nature or identity of something - 'what?'

questions.question: What does '¿Cuál prefieres?' mean?
questions.hint: '¿Cuál?' asks about choice or selection among options - 'which?'

questions.question: What does 'alguien' mean?
questions.hint: This is the indefinite pronoun for an unspecified person (positive).

questions.question: What does 'No veo a nadie' mean?

answers.text: I don't see anyone / I see no one

questions.hint: Spanish uses double negatives. 'No' + 'nadie' = negative statement (no one).

questions.question: What does 'algo' mean?
questions.hint: This is the indefinite pronoun for an unspecified thing (positive).

questions.question: What is the plural of 'you' in Latin America?
questions.hint: Latin America uses the same form for both formal and informal plural 'you'.
